paragraphs.context: At this school, you will be learning side by side with dragons
paragraphs.mainIdea: A school for all the tribes.
paragraphs.simple: This page is a welcome letter from Jade Mountain Academy. Young dragons from all the tribes study there together, so the next pages give some facts about each tribe.

paragraphs.context: You have been assigned to a winglet with six other dragons;
paragraphs.mainIdea: Each student is in a winglet.
paragraphs.simple: Every student is put in a small class called a winglet, with six dragons from other tribes. The list of winglets comes on the next page.

background.note: At Jade Mountain Academy, a small class of seven dragonets, one from each tribe.

paragraphs.context: WE WISH YOU ALL THE POWER OF WINGS OF FIRE!
paragraphs.simple: The letter says the students are the hope for a long peace in Pyrrhia. It ends with a wish. "Wings of fire" is a phrase from the old Dragonet Prophecy; here it means "may you be strong and do great things".

paragraphs.context: Abilities: can survive a long time without water, poison enemies with the tips
paragraphs.simple: SandWings can live a long time without water. They can poison enemies with the end of their tail, like a scorpion, hide under the sand, and breathe fire.

paragraphs.context: Queen: since the end of the War of SandWing Succession, Queen Thorn
paragraphs.mainIdea: The SandWings have a new queen.
paragraphs.simple: There was a long war about who would be the SandWing queen. That war is over now, and Thorn is the queen.

background.note: The war that began when Queen Oasis died and her three daughters fought to be queen of the SandWings. Most of the tribes joined in.
Thorn is now queen of the SandWings.

paragraphs.context: Students at Jade Mountain: Arid, Onyx, Ostrich, Pronghorn, Qibli
paragraphs.simple: These are the five SandWing students at the school. Each tribe page ends with a list like this.

paragraphs.context: Abilities: can breathe fire (if warm enough), hold their breath for up
paragraphs.simple: MudWings can breathe fire when they are warm, stay under water or mud for an hour without breathing, and hide in mud. They are very strong.

paragraphs.context: Abilities: powerful fighters and fliers, can breathe fire
paragraphs.simple: SkyWings are strong fighters and fast fliers, and they can breathe fire.

paragraphs.context: Queen: Queen Ruby (although some dragons still support Queen Scarlet,
paragraphs.simple: Ruby is the SkyWing queen now. But some SkyWings still want Scarlet, the old queen who lost her throne. Scarlet may still be alive and hiding somewhere.

background.note: Ruby is Queen Scarlet's daughter. After Scarlet loses her throne, Ruby becomes queen of the SkyWings.
Queen Scarlet was the cruel queen of the SkyWings until she lost her throne. She liked to watch prisoners fight in her arena.

paragraphs.context: Description: blue or green or aquamarine scales; webs between their claws; gills
paragraphs.simple: SeaWings are blue or green. They have skin between their claws, gills for breathing under water, and stripes that glow in the dark.

paragraphs.context: Abilities: can withstand subzero temperatures and bright light, exhale a deadly frostbreath
paragraphs.simple: IceWings can live in very cold places and in bright light, and they breathe out frostbreath, a deadly freezing breath.

background.note: The deadly freezing breath of IceWings; it can freeze and kill other dragons.

paragraphs.context: Abilities: can camouflage their scales to blend into their surroundings;
paragraphs.simple: RainWings can change the colors of their scales to hide and match the things around them. They can also shoot deadly venom (poison) from their fangs.

paragraphs.context: Abilities: can breathe fire, disappear into dark shadows; once known for reading minds
paragraphs.simple: NightWings can breathe fire and hide in dark shadows. Long ago they were famous for reading minds and seeing the future, but the guide says they cannot do this anymore.

background.note: The power to hear what other dragons are thinking.

paragraphs.context: Queen: Queen Glory (see recent scrolls on the NightWing Exodus and
paragraphs.simple: Glory, the RainWing queen, is now the queen of the NightWings too. The page says you can read about how this happened in new scrolls: the NightWings left their old home (the Exodus), and there was a contest for the RainWing throne.

background.note: Glory is a RainWing, one of the five dragonets of the prophecy. She is the queen of the RainWings, and now of the NightWings too.
The time when the NightWings left their island home.
The contest for the RainWing throne.

paragraphs.context: Beware the darkness of dragons,
paragraphs.simple: This is the Jade Mountain Prophecy, a new message about the future. It starts with warnings. "Beware" means "be careful of". "The darkness of dragons" means dragons who are evil or dangerous. "The stalker of dreams" is someone who follows dragons secretly, even in their dreams.

paragraphs.context: Beware the talons of power and fire,
paragraphs.simple: "Talons" are a dragon's claws. "The talons of power and fire" means a strong, dangerous dragon. The next line warns about a female dragon who is not what she seems: she hides who she really is.

paragraphs.context: Something is coming to shake the earth,
paragraphs.simple: Something terrible is coming. It will shake the ground and burn it. The prophecy does not say what it is.

paragraphs.context: Jade Mountain will fall beneath thunder and ice
paragraphs.simple: Here "fall" means "be destroyed". Jade Mountain, where the school is, will be destroyed by thunder and ice, unless dragons can find "the lost city of night". The prophecy does not say what the thunder and ice are, or where that city is.

background.note: A tall mountain in the middle of Pyrrhia with many caves inside it.

paragraphs.context: It was one of those days so blue and sunny
paragraphs.simple: The sky is blue and the wind is strong. It feels like a day when you must fly, because a day this perfect may never come again.

paragraphs.context: Hailstorm did a flip in the air, laughing. “The currents
paragraphs.simple: Hailstorm flips in the air and laughs. He shouts that he is the commander of the sky.

background.note: Hailstorm is Winter's older brother, an IceWing prince.

paragraphs.context: “I think the SkyWings would disagree,” Winter called. He twisted
paragraphs.simple: Winter reminds him that this is SkyWing land. He looks around the empty sky for danger.

background.note: Red and orange dragons with huge wings who live in the mountains of the Sky Kingdom. They are strong fighters and fast fliers.
Winter is an IceWing prince and a student at Jade Mountain Academy. He is proud and often cold to others.

paragraphs.context: “Stop worrying!” Hailstorm said, spinning into a dive. There weren’t
paragraphs.simple: No dragons are near. This is Winter's first trip into SkyWing land, and he wants to find a scavenger.

background.note: Dragons call humans 'scavengers'. In these books scavengers are small, clever people whom dragons often see as pests or pets.

paragraphs.context: “SHHHHHH,” Winter protested. “This is the Sky Kingdom! There could
paragraphs.simple: Winter tells his brother to be quiet. The Sky Kingdom belongs to their enemies, and there could be soldiers anywhere.

background.note: The land of the SkyWings, high in the mountains.

paragraphs.simple: Hailstorm thinks there is no danger. Winter is only three. Hailstorm likes him and enjoys teasing him, but he worries that Winter has trouble with the IceWing rankings.

background.note: A place where scavengers (humans) live together, such as a town or castle.

paragraphs.simple: Hailstorm reminds Winter that scavengers cannot live in the cold Ice Kingdom, so Winter cannot keep one.

background.note: The cold, snowy land of the IceWings in the far north.

background.note: Queen Scarlet was the cruel queen of the SkyWings until she lost her throne. She liked to watch prisoners fight in her arena.

paragraphs.simple: Hailstorm does not care about their parents. Queen Glacier has said he will be second-in-command of the IceWing army one day.

background.note: Queen Glacier is the queen of the IceWings.
Silver-white or pale blue dragons from the frozen north of Pyrrhia. They can live in great cold and breathe out a deadly freezing breath (frostbreath).

paragraphs.simple: Hailstorm says that dragons in the lower circles follow orders, but First Circle dragons must learn to lead. He thinks he can fight a few SkyWings.

parts.meaning: Winter thought it was odd

parts.text: that Hailstorm’s death could still hurt so much
parts.meaning: that Hailstorm dying could still cause so much pain
each time he believed it again.

sentences.grammar: "It was strange that…" puts the real subject (the that-clause) at the end of the sentence.

sentences.context: She said he’d been mourned already, and her duty was to the yet-unlost lives of her subjects.
sentences.simple: Glacier said the tribe had already grieved for Hailstorm, and she must protect the subjects who were still alive.

parts.text: She said he’d been mourned already,
parts.meaning: Glacier said the IceWings had already grieved for him,
and her job as queen was to care for

parts.text: to the yet-unlost lives of her subjects.
parts.meaning: the IceWings who had not been lost yet.

sentences.grammar: "He’d been mourned" is past perfect passive: the grieving happened before. "Yet-unlost" means "not lost so far".

sentences.context: This is not about your place in the rankings.
sentences.simple: This is not about how high your ranking is.

parts.meaning: The real reason is not

parts.job: The thing he cares too much about.
parts.meaning: where you stand in the IceWing order.

sentences.grammar: "Be about something" means that something is the real subject or purpose.

sentences.context: They didn’t have time for the mystery of a NightWing who worked for a deposed SkyWing queen.
sentences.simple: They had no time to solve the puzzle of a NightWing working for a SkyWing queen who had lost her throne.

parts.meaning: They could not stop

parts.text: for the mystery of a NightWing
parts.meaning: to think about the puzzle of a NightWing

parts.text: who worked for a deposed SkyWing queen.
parts.meaning: who served a SkyWing queen who had been removed from power.

sentences.grammar: "Deposed" means removed from the throne. "Who worked…" is a relative clause describing the NightWing.

sentences.context: Pyrite was gone. Standing in her place … was Hailstorm.
sentences.simple: Pyrite had disappeared, and Hailstorm was standing where she had been.

parts.meaning: Pyrite no longer existed there.
In the same spot where she had been,
Hailstorm was there.

sentences.grammar: The second sentence is inverted: the subject "Hailstorm" comes last to make a dramatic surprise. "In her place" means "where she had been".

sentences.context: He wouldn’t abandon her, not even to save Hailstorm.
sentences.simple: He would not leave Kinkajou behind, even if that would help him save Hailstorm.

parts.meaning: He would not leave Kinkajou alone,
even for the purpose of rescuing his brother.

sentences.grammar: "Not even to…" adds the most extreme case. "To save" is an infinitive of purpose.

sentences.context: He was astonished to find that he couldn’t even consider that possibility.
sentences.simple: He was very surprised to discover that he could not even think about leaving her.

parts.meaning: He was very surprised
to discover that

parts.text: he couldn’t even consider that possibility.
parts.meaning: he was unable even to think about that choice.

sentences.grammar: "Astonished to find that…" is adjective + infinitive. "That possibility" points back to leaving Kinkajou.

sentences.context: It smells like freedom.
sentences.simple: This place gives a feeling of freedom.

parts.meaning: This town has the smell
of being free.

sentences.grammar: "Smell like + noun" compares; here it is a metaphor, because freedom has no real smell.

sentences.context: Freedom to be whoever you want to be, not who someone tells you you have to be.
sentences.simple: The freedom to be any dragon you choose, not the dragon others order you to be.

parts.text: Freedom to be whoever you want to be,
parts.meaning: The chance to be any kind of dragon you choose,

parts.text: not who someone tells you you have to be.
parts.meaning: instead of the dragon others say you must be.

sentences.grammar: This is a sentence fragment that explains the word "freedom" before it. "Whoever" means "any person who".

sentences.context: Didn’t everyone want to know where they fit into the world?
sentences.simple: Surely every dragon wanted to know their place in the world.

parts.meaning: Didn't all dragons wish to understand

parts.text: where they fit into the world?
parts.meaning: what their place in the world is?

sentences.grammar: A negative question ("Didn’t…?") expects the answer "yes". "Fit into" means belong in a place.

sentences.context: He’d wanted to step into Pyrite’s talons so he could understand Hailstorm — but he didn’t want to understand him this well.
sentences.simple: He had wanted to become Pyrite to understand Hailstorm, but now he understood him more than he wanted.

parts.text: He’d wanted to step into Pyrite’s talons
parts.meaning: He had hoped to experience being Pyrite
in order to understand his brother,

parts.text: but he didn’t want to understand him this well.
parts.meaning: but now he understood him too deeply.

sentences.grammar: "Step into someone’s talons" is the dragon form of the idiom "step into someone’s shoes": imagine being them.

sentences.context: In his experience, no good could come of adding vengeance to a dragon’s list of reasons to get up in the morning.
sentences.simple: Winter knew that giving a dragon a reason for revenge never led to anything good.

parts.meaning: From what he had seen,
nothing good could result from

parts.text: adding vengeance to a dragon’s list of reasons
parts.meaning: giving a dragon revenge as another reason

parts.text: to get up in the morning.
parts.meaning: to keep going each day.

sentences.grammar: "No good can come of + -ing" means the action leads to bad results. "Reasons to get up in the morning" means reasons for living.

sentences.context: It’s how things have to be.
sentences.simple: This is the way things must be.

parts.meaning: This is the way
life must be for him.

sentences.grammar: "Have to" shows necessity. Winter is trying to convince himself.

sentences.context: He would ice over the hole in his chest, the way he’d cleared out the Pyrite memories.
sentences.simple: He would hide his sadness by freezing it, just as he had pushed away Pyrite's memories.

parts.text: He would ice over the hole in his chest,
parts.meaning: He would cover his painful loneliness with ice,

parts.text: the way he’d cleared out the Pyrite memories.
parts.meaning: just as he had removed Pyrite's thoughts from his mind.

sentences.grammar: "The hole in his chest" is a metaphor for sadness. "The way" means "in the same way that".

sentences.context: In any case, if Winter were an animus dragon, building a wall like that would not have been his major contribution to IceWing society.
sentences.simple: Anyway, if Winter had animus power, he would not have chosen to build a wall as his great gift to the IceWings.

parts.meaning: Anyway,

parts.text: if Winter were an animus dragon,
parts.meaning: if Winter had animus magic,
making a wall of that kind

parts.text: would not have been his major contribution to IceWing society.
parts.meaning: would not have been his big gift to the tribe.

sentences.grammar: "If Winter were…" is an unreal (second) conditional. The -ing phrase "building a wall like that" is the subject.

sentences.context: It was actually completely terrifying to think that any dragon with magic could easily wipe out an entire tribe with just one enchanted object.
sentences.simple: It was frightening to imagine that a dragon with magic could destroy a whole tribe with one enchanted thing.
sentences.main: Winter sees the danger of animus magic.

parts.meaning: It was truly very frightening

parts.text: to think that any dragon with magic
parts.meaning: to imagine that a dragon with animus power

parts.text: could easily wipe out an entire tribe
parts.meaning: could destroy a whole tribe without trouble
using only one magic object.

sentences.grammar: "It was terrifying to think…" uses "it" as a placeholder; the real subject is "to think…". "Wipe out" means destroy completely.

sentences.context: I’m going to have to work harder than ever to climb back up the rankings now.
sentences.simple: Now I must work harder than ever before to rise in the rankings again.

parts.text: I’m going to have to work
parts.meaning: I will need to work
more than I have ever worked

parts.text: to climb back up the rankings now.
parts.meaning: to rise to a high place again.

sentences.grammar: "Going to have to" combines future and necessity. "Climb back up" means return to a higher place.

sentences.context: Perhaps Winter had rescued his brother from one terrible fate only to doom him to another.
sentences.simple: Maybe Winter had saved his brother from one terrible thing, but only to send him into another.

parts.text: Perhaps Winter had rescued his brother
parts.meaning: Maybe Winter had saved Hailstorm
from one awful future

parts.text: only to doom him to another.
parts.meaning: with the result that he faced a different awful future.

sentences.grammar: "Only to…" shows a disappointing result after an action. "Another" means "another terrible fate".

sentences.context: Sacrifice one brother to save the other.
sentences.simple: Let one brother die so the other can be saved.

parts.meaning: Give up one son,
so that the other son's future is saved.

sentences.grammar: This is a short fragment that sums up the plan. "The other" means the second of two.

sentences.context: He still had to go down like an IceWing warrior.
sentences.simple: Even if he lost, he must fall bravely like an IceWing warrior.

parts.meaning: Even so, he must

parts.text: go down like an IceWing warrior.
parts.meaning: lose or die bravely, as a true IceWing fighter would.

sentences.grammar: "Go down" here means be defeated. "Still" means "even so".

sentences.context: And I could be one of them soon.
sentences.simple: Soon I might be one of these frozen dragons.

parts.meaning: I might become
one of the frozen dragons before long.

sentences.grammar: "Could" shows a possibility. "Them" points back to the frozen dragons.

sentences.context: Of course his parents would choose Hailstorm.
sentences.simple: Naturally, his parents would pick Hailstorm to win.

parts.meaning: Naturally, as expected,
his parents would pick Hailstorm over him.

sentences.grammar: "Of course" shows something is expected. "Would choose" is the future seen from the past.

sentences.context: Because happiness is not where I am … it’s who I’m with.
sentences.simple: Happiness does not come from the place I am in, but from the dragons I am with.

parts.text: Because happiness is not where I am …
parts.meaning: Since being happy does not depend on my place …
it depends on the friends beside me.

sentences.grammar: "Where I am" and "who I’m with" are noun clauses used as complements. The pattern "not X … (but) Y" contrasts two ideas.

sentences.context: No one cares at all what happens to me.
sentences.simple: Nobody cares even a little what happens to me.

parts.meaning: Nobody is worried even a little
about my future.

sentences.grammar: "At all" makes the negative stronger. "What happens to me" is a noun clause.

sentences.context: He was a dragon who had friends from other tribes.
sentences.simple: He was a dragon with friends in other tribes.

parts.meaning: Winter was now a dragon

parts.text: who had friends from other tribes.
parts.meaning: with friends who were not IceWings.

sentences.grammar: "Who had…" is a relative clause that describes "a dragon". Compare it with his old self-description: "prince among IceWings".

sentences.context: This dragon could change everything.
sentences.simple: This dragon might change the whole world.

parts.meaning: The dragon he is watching
might make everything different.

sentences.grammar: "Could" shows possibility. The short sentence makes a strong ending.

sentences.context: wondering why everything was so very ruined
sentences.simple: Qibli is joking. He does not really think one old dragon ruined the whole world.
sentences.grammar: He says the opposite of what he means, so the line is a joke.

a bunch of.meaning: A lot of; a group of.
a bunch of.example: Just what I need right now — a bunch of glaciers slowing me down.
a bunch of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

a couple of.example: Even if we do get caught, I think I can take a couple of SkyWings.”
a couple of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

about to.meaning: Going to happen or do something very soon.
about to.example: Winter stepped back, tense, like a wolf about to spring.
about to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

according to.meaning: As said or shown by someone or something.
according to.example: It was instinct to see a NightWing and think of his brother’s death, but according to Queen Scarlet, Hailstorm wasn’t dead.
according to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

after all.meaning: In the end, even though you did not expect it.
after all.example: Maybe they weren’t completely wasting their time in here after all.
after all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

all along.meaning: 1. Along the whole length of something ("bruising all along her spine"). 2. The whole time, from the beginning.
all along.example: Sharp spikes shoved up through the skin all along her back and at the tip of her tail.
all along.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

all of a sudden.example: “Imagine being a totally different dragon all of a sudden,” Qibli said.
all of a sudden.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

all the way.example: Chains weighed down his talons and strange metal bands prevented his wings from unfurling all the way.
all the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

apart from.example: returned from battle as pristine as when she’d left, apart from a few bleeding blue scratches here and there.
apart from.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

as far as.meaning: "As far as she could tell" = from what she could see or know.
as far as.example: But as far as he could tell, there was no conscious thought involved.
as far as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that...
as if.example: He blinked at the trees, as if hoping a scavenger would suddenly fall out of one of them.
as if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

as long as.meaning: If; only if. (Also: for the whole time that.) "A spear as long as a dragon" = a spear that is the same length as a dragon.
as long as.example: As long as you’re holding it or wearing it close to your scales, I can’t hear anything you’re thinking.”
as long as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as soon as.example: “Heliconia, please tell my scout captains to meet me at the pavilion as soon as possible.”
as soon as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as though.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that something is true.
as though.example: Hailstorm ruffled his wings as though he was trying to shake the idea of their parents right off his scales.
as though.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at all.meaning: Used with "not", "no", "hardly" or in questions to mean "in any way" or "even a little". "Not at all" = not in any way.
at all.example: And then Bandit hadn’t appreciated it at all.
at all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at first.meaning: At the start, before something changes.
at first.example: The creature was wrapped in so many furs, at first Winter almost thought it was another polar bear cub.
at first.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at last.example: He’d bring home a polar bear at last, and if he hurried, it might even be him sitting next to
at last.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at least.meaning: Used to say one thing is good, even when other things are bad.
at least.example: “They said they saw at least five scavengers, and that many usually means a den nearby.”
at least.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at once.meaning: Immediately; or all at the same time.
at once.example: “In fact, if you don’t shut up at once, I will change my mind.”
at once.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at the same time.example: Qibli’s words had riled up the NightWings and made Winter feel better at the same time.
at the same time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

back and forth.meaning: First one way, then the other way, again and again.
back and forth.example: Glory’s tail lashed back and forth as she began issuing orders.
back and forth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

be supposed to.meaning: Should; to be expected to do something.
be supposed to.example: So did Winter, although he suspected he wasn’t supposed to.
be supposed to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

believe in.meaning: To think that something is real.
believe in.example: How could Moon be immersed in other minds all day and still believe in the goodness of dragons?
believe in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

burst into.meaning: To come into a place suddenly and fast. "Burst into tears" = suddenly start to cry.
burst into.example: the first time would be the worst — the night a spy had burst into the royal dining room, shouting that all of Scarlet’s
burst into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

by the way.meaning: You say "by the way" to start talking about something new.
by the way.example: on sight, or my brother, who might do the same because, by the way, killing SeaWings was a specialty of his.
by the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

calm down.meaning: To become calm, not excited or afraid.
calm down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch up.meaning: To come up to someone who is in front of you, by going faster.
catch up.example: When Winter caught up to the others, they were gathered at the base of a huge tree beside a waterfall, staring up at a hole in the trunk.
catch up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

change your mind.meaning: To make a different choice from before.
change your mind.example: “Right here, in case you change your mind and realize that stopping a big world-destroying prophecy is what you were hatched to do.”
change your mind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

chime in.meaning: To join a talk by saying something.
chime in.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

clear your throat.meaning: To cough a little before you speak.
clear your throat.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come on.meaning: "Come on!" = Please! or Hurry! (Also: something coming on = something starting: "I sense a terrible idea coming on.")
come on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come true.meaning: (Of a wish or dream) to really happen.
come true.example: “It seems like her dream come true.”
come true.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come up with.meaning: To think of an idea or plan.
come up with.example: “I had no idea they could come up with something like that.”
come up with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

deal with.meaning: To take action to handle a problem or a difficult feeling.
deal with.example: I can’t use him in my arena if I want to trade him later, and I don’t want to deal with any messy escape or rescue attempts.”
deal with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

each other.meaning: Used to say that each one does something to the other one.
each other.example: “Although there’s something a little ominous about ‘darkness’ and ‘stalker’ so close to each other in the prophecy.
each other.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

end up.meaning: To be in a place or situation at the end, often without planning it.
end up.example: They’d end up dead if they did; she was bigger, more ferocious, and ten times better trained than any of these little dragons.
end up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

even if.meaning: It does not matter if this happens; the result is the same.
even if.example: Even if we do get caught, I think I can take a couple of SkyWings.”
even if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

even though.meaning: Although; in spite of the fact that.
even though.example: “He’s still having nightmares about the volcano every night, even though that was months ago.
even though.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

fall asleep.example: Winter arranged himself in the IceWing guarding stance, but after a while all his training failed and he fell asleep.
fall asleep.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

feel like.meaning: To seem like; to give a certain feeling. "Feel like doing something" = want to do it.
feel like.example: His heart felt like the rock in his talons, small and hard.
feel like.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

feel sorry for.meaning: To feel sad for someone who has a problem.
feel sorry for.example: Did it feel sorry for them, too?
feel sorry for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

figure out.meaning: To find the answer to something by thinking.
figure out.example: There were hundreds of furry smells in the forest, but he couldn’t even figure out which ones were scavengers and which ones were squirrels.
figure out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know.
find out.example: “Try to find out more about what Scarlet told her.”
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

for a moment.example: She studied him for a moment, and then an unexpected smile quirked the corners of her mouth.
for a moment.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for instance.example: wiser gift in the eyes of other tribes — RainWings, for instance, who took care of one another so easily and had
for instance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

for sure.example: Stronger than anyone else here, that’s for sure.
for sure.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get away with.meaning: To do something wrong and not be punished for it.
get away with.example: He couldn’t let a NightWing treat him that way, especially in front of all the other NightWings, and get away with it.
get away with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get out of.meaning: To leave a place; or to find a way to avoid doing something.
get out of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get rid of.meaning: To make something go away; to be free of it.
get rid of.example: Which meant Winter could get rid of him by applying the right pressure.
get rid of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

give up.meaning: 1. To stop trying. 2. To give something up = to stop having it, or to hand it over ("give up your place in the rankings").
give up.example: Why had it lowered its spear as if it was already giving up?
give up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go on.meaning: To continue; to keep talking ("Qibli went on"). "Going on" = happening ("What's going on?" = what is happening?). "Go on!" = go now, or do it ("Go on, sleep"). "Go on ahead" = go first, before the others. "Go on a mission" = go away to do a mission ("I went on my first mission").
go on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

grow up.meaning: To change from a child into an adult.
grow up.example: “This is where I grew up,” she said, wading a few steps into the river.
grow up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

had better.meaning: Should. "We'd better go" means we should go now. (Different: "had better night vision" = had night vision that was better.)
had better.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hang on.meaning: To hold something tightly. "Hang on!" can also mean "Wait!"
hang on.example: “Hang on — let me see the paper.”
hang on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

have a feeling.meaning: To think something is true or will happen, without knowing for sure.
have a feeling.example: But I wouldn’t be here now if it weren’t for my friends, and I have a feeling you’ll be saying the same thing a year from now.”
have a feeling.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

i bet.example: “I bet Pyrite is a kind of mask,” Moon offered.
i bet.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

i guess.meaning: "I guess" means "I think so, but I am not sure."
i guess.example: I guess some dragons are just —”
i guess.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

i mean.meaning: You say it when you want to say something again in a better way.
i mean.example: “If we stick to your … unusual specifications, I mean.”
i mean.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

if only.meaning: "If only ..." means "I wish ..." (but it is not true).
if only.example: The look that said, if only we’d lost you instead of Hailstorm.
if only.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in case.example: To hide from him, in case he ever came back.”
in case.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in charge.meaning: Being the one who decides and controls things.
in charge.example: of a dragon she couldn’t trust and wouldn’t want to see in charge of the Sky Kingdom again anyway.
in charge.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in exchange for.meaning: Given or done to pay for something else.
in exchange for.example: She’d agreed to kill the dragonets of destiny in exchange for Hailstorm … but Winter had stopped her.
in exchange for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in fact.meaning: Really; actually (used to add something true and surprising).
in fact.example: He made the top of the list the same day Icicle and Winter hatched, in fact.
in fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in front of.example: “Don’t be a mewling RainWing in front of our enemies.”
in front of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in order to.meaning: So that you can; for the purpose of.
in order to.example: gone off to find a dragon who just tried to kill you, in order to find another dragon who has tried to kill you about
in order to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in the end.example: “You’ll be our prisoners in the end, either way.”
in the end.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in the first place.meaning: At the beginning; before anything else.
in the first place.example: We must also factor in the clumsiness of allowing himself to be caught by SkyWings in the first place.”
in the first place.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in your head.example: What have you seen in my head?
in your head.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

instead of.meaning: In the place of something else.
instead of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

keep an eye on.example: Go keep an eye on Jade Mountain instead.”
keep an eye on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

keep track of.meaning: To always know where something is or what is happening.
keep track of.example: Winter tried to keep track of the hours in his head, calculating when it would be dawn.
keep track of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep up.meaning: To go as fast as someone else; to continue doing something.
keep up.example: Winter couldn’t imagine how the SandWing could even take off with her on top of him, let alone keep up a breakneck escape pace.
keep up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

kind of.meaning: 1. A type of ("what kind of animal"; "the kind of dragon who..."). 2. A little; in some way (informal): "kind of grouchy".
kind of.example: “That’s absolutely our favorite kind of prisoner.
kind of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

leave alone.meaning: To not touch, change or bother someone or something.
leave alone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

leave behind.meaning: To go away and not take someone or something with you.
leave behind.example: He’s gone — this is just the shape of him left behind.”
leave behind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let go of.example: Moon let go of him and took a shaky breath.
let go of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

let out.meaning: 1. To make a sound, such as a cry or a sigh. 2. To let someone or something out = to allow them to leave or go out ("let me out").
let out.example: Suddenly Moon let out a yell of pain and crumpled forward, her wings collapsing around her.
let out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

look around.meaning: To look at the things in a place, or to look in all directions.
look around.example: The dragon next to him looked around in alarm, spotted Winter, and leaped backward, nearly knocking one of her companions off the platform.
look around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look like.meaning: To seem to be something, because of how it looks.
look like.example: Moon closed her eyes, then shook her head with an expression that looked like frustration.
look like.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make friends with.meaning: To start to be friends with someone.
make friends with.example: I do not make friends with dragons from other tribes.
make friends with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make sense.meaning: To be easy to understand; to seem right.
make sense.example: Following Icicle would make sense, except …
make sense.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

make sure.meaning: To check, or to do something, so that you are sure about something.
make sure.example: He glanced back only once, as they were all swooping away, to make sure it was all right.
make sure.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

make up for.meaning: To do something good so that something bad seems less bad.
make up for.example: I hope you intend to be exceptionally thrilling now to make up for it.”
make up for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no idea.meaning: "Have no idea" means not know at all.
no idea.example: Now that they were surrounded by trees, though, he had no idea how they were going to find one of the little creatures for Winter.
no idea.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no longer.meaning: Not now, although it was true before.
no longer.example: Abilities: can breathe fire, disappear into dark shadows; once known for reading minds and foretelling the future, but no longer
no longer.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no matter what.example: No matter what they said, they wouldn’t change his mind.
no matter what.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no sign of.meaning: Nothing that shows someone is there.
no sign of.example: “I’ve been listening as hard as I can since we got to the rainforest, but there’s no sign of her.”
no sign of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no way.meaning: 1. That can't be true! 2. Certainly not. 3. "There is no way to..." = it is impossible to...
no way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no wonder.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

of course.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, dear.meaning: What you say when you are worried, sorry or a little upset about something. It does not mean "loved" here.
oh, dear.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, my.meaning: What you say when you are surprised or shocked, like "Oh!" or "Wow!" Here "my" does not mean "belonging to me". ("Oh my gosh!" and "Oh my goodness!" mean the same.)
oh, my.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

on fire.example: “The NightWings are going to set their heads on fire,” Qibli agreed.
on fire.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

on purpose.meaning: Because you want to; not by accident.
on purpose.example: On purpose, even though he wants to be with her as badly as I do.
on purpose.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

on your own.meaning: Alone, without help from other people.
on your own.example: One might even infer that somebody doesn’t think he can do his job properly on his own.
on your own.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

one another.example: basic information that may be useful as you get to know one another.
one another.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

one by one.example: They landed one by one, shaking out their wings and sinking their talons into the clawmarked wooden floor.
one by one.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

out loud.meaning: In a voice that other people can hear.
out loud.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

out of the way.meaning: Not standing where someone wants to go.
out of the way.example: “Then get out of the way and let me out,” Winter said in a strangled voice that came out more harshly than he’d meant it to.
out of the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

over and over.example: “So you just get murdered over and over again?”
over and over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pick up.meaning: To lift something up with your hand.
pick up.example: She picked up the drawing and held it close to her chest.
pick up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

plenty of.meaning: A lot of; more than enough.
plenty of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

point of view.meaning: The way you see or think about something.
point of view.example: The NightWing who was already too close to her brother, from Icicle’s point of view.
point of view.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

point out.meaning: To tell someone about something so that they see it or know it.
point out.example: Qibli pointed out, flicking his tail at Winter, “that’ll actually bring you
point out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

reach out.meaning: To move your hand forward to touch or take something.
reach out.example: Moon landed next to Winter and suddenly reached out to brush his wing with hers.
reach out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

right away.example: he had the power to read minds, he’d tell other dragons right away instead of invading their minds in secret.
right away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

roll one's eyes.meaning: To move your eyes up and around, to show that you think something is silly.
roll one's eyes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

run away.meaning: To leave a place secretly or quickly to escape.
run away.example: Mostly he’d cowered under the furs and squeaked, or he’d tried to run away.
run away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

scavenger den.meaning: A town or castle where scavengers (humans) live together.
scavenger den.example: “Lounging around in the woods near a scavenger den?”
scavenger den.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

shake your head.meaning: To move your head from side to side to say "no" or to show you are unhappy.
shake your head.example: Moon shook her head and pressed herself upright, her wings unsteady.
shake your head.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

side by side.example: At this school, you will be learning side by side with dragons from all the other tribes, so we wanted to
side by side.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

so far.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

sort of.meaning: 1. A type of; something like ("What sort of sinister plans"; "a sort of pale jade green"). 2. A little; not completely. (Informal.)
sort of.example: let them pass, smirking in a horribly superior NightWing sort of way.
sort of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

stay away from.example: “I’ll stay away from the Ice Kingdom.”
stay away from.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

step forward.meaning: To move one step to the front.
step forward.example: Winter took a step forward as Moon emerged behind him and breathed out a small plume of fire.
step forward.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to feel calm.
take a deep breath.example: He took a deep breath, inhaling the smells of the forest, and sneezed loudly.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take a step back.meaning: To move back one step, often because you are surprised or afraid.
take a step back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take care of.meaning: To look after someone or something and keep them safe.
take care of.example: “Maybe he didn’t want to leave them all alone with no mummy to take care of them, poor wittle furballs.”
take care of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take over.example: I thought for a while I was having visions of a possible future where newts and anteaters took over the world.”
take over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

tell the truth.meaning: To say what is really true, not a lie.
tell the truth.example: “Winter, I think she’s telling the truth,” Moon said.
tell the truth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

thank the moons.meaning: A dragon way of saying "Thank goodness!"
thank the moons.example: “Thank the moons,” Winter said, leaping to his feet.
thank the moons.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the rest of.example: To his astonishment, it was the rest of his winglet from the Jade Mountain Academy: Qibli, Turtle, Kinkajou … and Moon.
the rest of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

three moons.meaning: "Three moons!" is an exclamation, like "Oh my goodness!" (It can also mean the three real moons in the dragons' sky.)
three moons.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

trail off.meaning: (Of a voice) to slowly become quieter and stop.
trail off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn out.meaning: To happen in the end in a way you did not expect. "Turned out to be" means were, as people learned later.
turn out.example: was secretly conspiring with Queen Scarlet because it turns out Winter’s brother is, like, actually alive, not dead like
turn out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

used to.meaning: Did something regularly in the past, but not now. "Be used to" = know something well, so it is not strange.

used to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

wake up.example: He woke up in a bright throne room, so bright he instantly got a headache, although the brightness of the sun on ice had never bothered him.
wake up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

what if.example: “But what if the mountain falls on me?
what if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

who cares.meaning: It doesn't matter; I don't care.
who cares.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

think of.meaning: To have an idea come into your mind, or to remember or consider something.
think of.example: It was instinct to see a NightWing and think of his brother’s death, but according to Queen Scarlet, Hailstorm wasn’t dead.

burst out.meaning: To come out of a place suddenly and with force. It can also mean to say something suddenly.
burst out.example: A fat orange toad burst out of the river and made a clumsy dash for the reeds, trying to get away from the dragons.

listen to.meaning: To pay attention to what someone says or to a sound.
listen to.example: “I think I’d probably rather die in battle than listen to my brother talk about me that way.”

hold out.meaning: To stretch out your arm, hand or claw in front of you.

look for.example: “I’m going to look for my brother.”

stand up.meaning: To get up onto your feet. It can also mean to point straight up.

step back.example: “Didn’t realize he was with you, Meerkat.” He took a step back.

let go.example: Moon let go of him and took a shaky breath.

be about to.meaning: To be ready to do something very soon.

your majesty.meaning: A polite title for a queen or a king.

stick together.example: Better to stick together and know for sure.

by accident.example: “If you ever get stabbed by my tail, I promise it won’t be by accident,” Qibli said haughtily.

watch out.example: And I did promise Mother to watch out for Anemone, so I should, uh, I should really do that, you know?

polar opposite.meaning: The total opposite. As different as something can be.
polar opposite.example: It must be the polar opposite of the Ice Kingdom.

higgledy piggledy.meaning: All mixed up, with no order.
higgledy piggledy.example: We would never allow such higgledy-piggledy shenanigans in the Ice Kingdom.

seal guts.meaning: An angry shout. Winter says it when something goes badly wrong.
seal guts.example: “It attacked me and stole my prey and then disapp — oh, SEAL GUTS!”

present company excepted.meaning: Everyone here is not included in the unkind thing just said.

by any chance.meaning: Maybe. Used when you ask if something is possible.
by any chance.example: Can you by any chance remember about a week ago when someone tried to eat your pet?”

off limits.meaning: Not allowed. You must not touch it or go there.
